title: Kotlin Foundations
description: General Kotlin practice for mobile engineers, focused on reasoning, safe code, and interview-ready fundamentals.

courses.title: Kotlin for Mobile Engineers
courses.description: Learn the language decisions behind readable Android and multiplatform code without starting in a full IDE.

chapters.title: Unit 1 · Syntax and values
chapters.summary: Use val, var, data classes, enums, and when expressions with intent.

lessons.title: Model everyday app data
lessons.explanation: Kotlin makes common data decisions explicit. Practise the smallest syntax that keeps intent visible.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword declares a read-only reference?
exercises.explanation: val prevents reassignment of the reference after initialization.

exercises.prompt: What does a data class generate for value-like data?
exercises.code: data class Profile(val id: String, val displayName: String)
exercises.explanation: Data classes generate useful value semantics and a copy function.

exercises.prompt: What is a when expression required to provide?
options: An exhaustive set of branches or else
exercises.explanation: When used as an expression, Kotlin must know that a value is produced for every case.

exercises.prompt: What is an enum class useful for?
options: A fixed set of named states
exercises.explanation: Enums make a closed set of named states visible to the compiler and reader.

exercises.prompt: What does type inference do?
options: Kotlin deduces a type from the expression
exercises.explanation: Kotlin can infer many types without losing static checking.

exercises.prompt: Why prefer val when a value does not need reassignment?
options: It communicates stable intent and reduces accidental mutation
It always makes the object deeply immutable
exercises.explanation: Read-only references make data flow easier to reason about, even when nested objects can still mutate.

exercises.prompt: What does a function expression return?
options: The value of its final expression
exercises.explanation: Kotlin functions can use the final expression as their return value.

exercises.prompt: What is a good first question in an unfamiliar Kotlin problem?
options: What is the input, output, and boundary behavior?
Can every line be one expression?
exercises.explanation: A clear contract turns syntax selection into a testable reasoning decision.

chapters.title: Unit 2 · Null safety
chapters.summary: Handle absent data with nullable types, safe calls, Elvis defaults, and smart casts.

lessons.title: Make absence explicit
lessons.explanation: Nullable types turn missing data into a visible branch instead of a surprise crash.

exercises.prompt: What does String? mean?
exercises.explanation: The question mark marks a nullable type that can hold a String or null.

exercises.prompt: What does profile?.displayName return if profile is null?
exercises.explanation: The safe-call operator short-circuits to null when the receiver is null.

exercises.prompt: How do you provide a fallback of Guest when nickname is null?
exercises.explanation: The Elvis operator returns its right side when the left side is null.

exercises.prompt: What is the purpose of let on a nullable value?
options: Run a block only when the value is non-null
exercises.explanation: value?.let { } is useful for scoping work to the non-null branch.

exercises.prompt: Why should !! be used sparingly?
options: It can throw if the value is null
It changes a val to var
It is slower than every other operator
exercises.explanation: The not-null assertion moves the null failure to runtime.

exercises.prompt: What is a smart cast?
options: The compiler remembers a successful type or null check
A cast performed by the network
exercises.explanation: After a safe check, Kotlin can use the refined type in the guarded branch.

exercises.prompt: What should a UI do when remote data is absent?
options: Represent an intentional empty or loading state
exercises.explanation: Absence is a product state that should be rendered or recovered from intentionally.

exercises.prompt: What is the safest default for data from an API?
options: Validate it before treating it as a non-null domain value
exercises.explanation: Validation keeps untrusted data from leaking unsafe assumptions into the rest of the app.

chapters.title: Unit 3 · Collections
chapters.summary: Transform lists and maps while keeping mutability and intent clear.

lessons.title: Transform app data
lessons.explanation: Kotlin collection operations read like a small data pipeline: filter what matters, map it, then combine it when needed.

exercises.prompt: What does listOf return?
exercises.explanation: listOf creates a read-only List view; use mutableListOf when mutation is required.

exercises.prompt: Which operation keeps elements that match a predicate?
exercises.explanation: filter returns only elements whose predicate is true.

exercises.prompt: Which operation changes each element into another value?
exercises.explanation: map applies a transformation to every element.

exercises.prompt: What does reduce commonly produce?
exercises.explanation: reduce combines elements into one accumulated value such as a sum.

exercises.prompt: Which collection is designed for unique values?
exercises.explanation: Set removes duplicate membership and supports set-style operations.

exercises.prompt: What does associateBy help create?
options: A map keyed by a selected property
exercises.explanation: associateBy is useful when later code needs keyed lookup by a domain property.

exercises.prompt: When is a Sequence worth considering?
options: When lazy chained processing can avoid intermediate collections
exercises.explanation: Sequences evaluate lazily and can help with larger pipelines, but they add a trade-off.

exercises.prompt: What should you ask before choosing a MutableList?
options: Who owns the mutation and whether it is necessary
Whether the list has a title
exercises.explanation: Mutation is an ownership decision; a read-only interface is often safer at boundaries.

chapters.title: Unit 4 · Coroutines
chapters.summary: Read suspend functions, structured concurrency, cancellation, and UI dispatch as decisions.

lessons.title: Make asynchronous work visible
lessons.explanation: Coroutines let code describe asynchronous work without hiding its lifecycle. The scope that starts work should own its cancellation.

exercises.prompt: What does suspend mean on a function?
options: It may pause without blocking the underlying thread
It always creates a new thread
exercises.explanation: A suspend function can pause and resume within a coroutine.

exercises.prompt: What is structured concurrency trying to preserve?
options: A parent scope owns child work and its lifetime
All work runs on the UI thread
exercises.explanation: Structured concurrency keeps work tied to a scope so cancellation and failures are understandable.

exercises.prompt: What should happen when a screen is destroyed?
options: Its screen-owned coroutine work should be cancelled
Its requests should keep updating hidden UI
It should block the main thread
exercises.explanation: Lifecycle-aware scopes prevent stale work from writing into a screen that no longer exists.

exercises.prompt: What is Dispatchers.Main for?
options: UI work that must run on the main thread
exercises.explanation: UI frameworks require main-thread access for view state updates.

exercises.prompt: What does withContext usually communicate?
options: Run a block in a different coroutine context
exercises.explanation: withContext makes a context switch explicit and returns the block's result.

exercises.prompt: Why should coroutine errors be handled at a meaningful boundary?
options: The UI or caller can choose recovery
exercises.explanation: Error handling belongs where the product can decide whether to retry, show, or ignore the failure.

exercises.prompt: What is a race between two requests?
options: Results arrive in an order different from user intent
Two values have the same type
exercises.explanation: Request identity or cancellation keeps older work from overwriting newer intent.

exercises.prompt: What is a good default for network data before rendering it?
options: Represent loading, success, empty, and error states
exercises.explanation: Explicit states make async UI behavior predictable for learners and users.

chapters.title: Unit 5 · Testing and interviews
chapters.summary: Test boundaries, explain trade-offs, and communicate the simplest correct solution.

lessons.title: Prove the behavior
lessons.explanation: Good tests name a behavior and make edge cases visible. Good interviews explain the same choices out loud.

exercises.prompt: Which argument comes first in assertEquals(expected, actual)?
exercises.explanation: JUnit convention places the known expected value first.

exercises.prompt: What is a boundary test?
options: A test for empty, smallest, largest, or unusual valid input
A test for a private variable name
exercises.explanation: Boundary cases expose off-by-one and missing-state errors that happy paths miss.

exercises.prompt: What makes a function easy to unit test?
options: Explicit inputs, deterministic output, and few hidden dependencies
exercises.explanation: Pure or dependency-injected functions are easier to exercise and explain.

exercises.prompt: What should you clarify before coding an interview problem?
options: Input, output, constraints, and edge cases
exercises.explanation: A clear contract prevents solving the wrong problem and provides test cases.

exercises.prompt: What is a useful invariant?
options: A fact that stays true while the algorithm progresses
exercises.explanation: Naming the invariant explains why the algorithm remains correct after each step.

exercises.prompt: When should you prefer a simpler algorithm?
options: When constraints do not require extra complexity
Only when it has more lines
exercises.explanation: Complexity has a maintenance cost, so it should answer a real constraint.

exercises.prompt: What is the best reason to use a sealed class for UI state?
options: It makes a closed set of states explicit and exhaustively handled
exercises.explanation: Sealed hierarchies help the compiler and reader see every supported state.

exercises.prompt: How should you explain a Kotlin design choice in an interview?
options: Connect it to correctness, readability, performance, or maintainability
exercises.explanation: The strongest answers connect language features to the constraint they solve.
